to live in poverty. This was your first intention. The fear of God is not before your eyes. You think nothing of the salvation of souls. You have no understanding of eternal life. You desire to walk in the pleasure of the flesh alone. All the causes and reasons that you related in your petition are fabricated and false. How will the dispensation be lawful? How will the authority of the supreme pontiff excuse you, which you did not fear to circumvent by falsehood, fraud, deceit, and importunate prayers? What should be thought of you, your conduct, once examined, has declared. For the Lord says in the Gospel about ravening wolves: By their fruits you shall know them. Never is true joy seen among you because of it; never can the conscience be secure, but it is always anxious over its guilt, always troubled, since they have the devil as an inciter to despair, by whose prompting you have withdrawn from the order of necessity. Hence it is that you are not at all solicitous about the love of God and the salvation of souls, but, intent on earthly vanities and carnal desires, you think of nothing less than eternal life. By what spirit this transfer was made among you, your way of life shows. For those who are led by the spirit of God have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires. But you are not so. For as soon as you cast off the habit of religion, like wanton oxen, released from the yoke of subjection, you plunge yourselves, as if lawfully, into every disgrace; you cast off all honor; you make a pact with vices and wage war against virtues. The charity of God is not in your hearts. You despise mercy and piety. You love vanity, and you have become vain. You are evil to all good men, worse to monks, worst to yourselves. A transfer that has opened an entrance to vices has not been made for the better. Deserters of the love of God and of the order, enemies of honor, adversaries of piety: if you love God, if you are good, if you love religion, why do you hate monks? But you hate especially those who have persevered in the order from which you have fallen away, because, when you see those men now standing firmly in their vocation, you fear their testimony against you in judgment. Therefore all monks persevering in holy conduct will stand in the strict examination, about to bear testimony against you; by their works they will show that all the accounts and causes of your apostasy, already here cloaked in fraudulent words, are false and empty. You hate the monks of your order because, in truth, as you know yourselves to be, so you judge others to be; and the good that you do not see in yourselves, you also envy in others. We do not wonder at the madness of your heart against monks, when we consider the injury and insult that you have brought upon God and upon your holy lawgiver. For one who does not love God, who breaks the vow solemnly made to him, who casts off the habit of religion, is not to be wondered at if he hates the monks who are his servants. For every apostate is an adversary and despiser of his order. But I beg, but I exhort, but I urge all of you who have deserted your order: abandon fury, soften your rage, cease to rave against monks, lest those whom you now persecute with hatred you have in judgment as witnesses and judges against you. Do penance for this impiety of yours while you have time, lest swift death seize you unprepared. Do not, I beseech you, vent the corruption of malice against Saint Benedict; do not wish, by your transfers, to destroy his venerable order; do not despise the opportunity for repentance, if you desire to attain eternal life. You have built no monastery for Saint Benedict. I ask and exhort you not to transfer to the uses of secular men those built for him by others. Remember how brief the present life is, how certain death is, how strict the judge is; and do not place upon your necks so heavy a burden of sacrilege that you will never be able to restore it worthily by any satisfaction. Do not stir up Saint Benedict as an adversary against you, if you desire to find the friendship of the other saints. For when one has been offended, none of the rest will be a friend. Consider the end of those who long ago transferred themselves from the holy order, and likewise fear for your own. Where are the abbots and monks who once withdrew from the order and handed over the monasteries of the holy father Benedict into the hands of secular men? [unclear] They are either dead, or shortly will die. You also who still live, who, following the example of those before you, have withdrawn from the order, [unclear] think that you will go to those whose imitators you are.

for you would fear for yourselves from another’s peril, and, while there is time, would take up penance with your whole heart. I have heard from many with how great bitterness of mind, at the point of death, many transgressors of the order have been constrained: those who from monks became canons, or also those who were the authors of transfers of this sort. For they said that they grieved for no sin so much as for that one, because they knew that they had given their consent, or their help, to the transfer of the order. If the transfer of monasteries from the order is good, why did those who had made it grieve when they were dying? But if it is evil, why do you make it and take it upon yourselves? Let all who occupy the monasteries of monks remember how stern an anathema they are marked with by blessed Pope Gregory: those who do not fear to turn the property of monasteries consecrated to God to alien uses. Let Thietgandus, formerly archbishop of [Trier?], be an example to them: when he had received from Pope Adrian, in the city of Rome, the monastery of Saint Andrew in [unclear], and, after that had been [unclear], had been warned by Saint Gregory in a third vision not to occupy the dwellings of monks any longer, since, when ordered to withdraw, he ignored it, he perished with all his people by a hard death. Whether those who occupy the monasteries of monks are secure before God, we leave to their consciences. But he who possesses another man’s goods without that man’s will is bound to restitution; whoever occupies the goods of some saint against his will, let him consider what he deserves. We have now used a sufficiently long discourse against the transgressors of our order; and so let us now come to the things that remain.

Chapter V.

How these dismemberments of apostate monks are to be opposed.

Although both my mind and necessity itself, having been constrained, offer an abundance of material for inveighing against the destroyers of our order, nevertheless, since those are not present who might be recalled to penance by exhortations, I think that enough has been said against them. For they are senseless, those who so wickedly oppress the honor of their order; and I judge that they must be resisted not only with words, but with deeds. For those who do not fear God will by no means acquiesce in our admonitions. Come then, most reverend fathers, who have assembled in chapter for the adornment of our order, who labor for its restoration: recall to mind its former state, and consider into how great a calamity it has fallen in this time. Behold, monasteries are snatched from the hands of Saint Benedict; our order is being destroyed all around by the enemies of God; monks return to the world; the impious tear apart our religion; strangers are endowed with our goods. What shall I say of internal wars? What shall I report of civil evils? It is no wonder, fathers, take heed, if we are confounded without, since we are torn apart within by our own people. Our abbots kick against discipline, tear apart the unity of the order, neglect the statutes of chapters, spurn visitations, and despise your censures, fathers. Unless you fight against these men with all censures [unclear] to bring back [unclear] under the order for long. Why then do you dissemble? How long do you sleep? When will you wake up? When will you fight for the inheritance of Saint Benedict? Fathers, arm yourselves with zeal for God, for order, and for discipline, because it is time; fight for your lawful rights; defend the rights of sanctity. Stand manfully against transfers of the order. Behold, from our order in the province of Mainz alone six monasteries have already been transferred in our times; and unless we keep watch otherwise, we shall suffer more grievous losses day by day. Thus, while we dissemble, not to say grow torpid, the order is gradually diminished, until at last it will be entirely scattered. Why do we not meet such great dangers? Or, while the others perish, do we wisely trust in our own security? Did not the poet truly say: your affair is at stake when the nearest wall is burning? Yesterday it was for them; tomorrow a like danger will threaten us. Each one of you, I do not doubt, loves his own monastery, and would in no way consent that it be transferred from the order; indeed, he would wish not only its present but also its future happiness to be extended for eternal years. Why, then, do you not defend in common what you fear to lose individually? I fear, fathers, that in this most evil dissembling our tenacity may be accused. We love money and lose a monastery. We fear a few expenses and lose broad dwellings. We are unwilling to lay out a modest sum of money, and we suffer most abundant monasteries to pass from the order to outsiders. Private advantages [are preferred?] to the common utility

we do not take care to preserve the honor of the order. We say much; we conclude much in favor of the useful defense of the order, but we are afraid to lay out all the money. O feeble zeal, which tenacity renders useless. If we will not give money for our brothers, when shall we expose our life? If we do not contribute a few expenses for the preservation of the order, when shall we give our bodies? He who is grasping in a small matter, when will he be generous in a great one?

I shall now speak to you, fathers, who pretend not to notice that the order has been placed in such great dangers and needs help. Blessed Benedict made you rich from poor men; now he asks alms from you, and, shameful to say, does not receive them. Behold how many there are among us, if I may say so with pardon, who divide their substance among frivolous persons, prepare banquets for birds and dogs, enrich their parents and kinsmen from the goods of the monastery, and squander the rest on empty pleasures. Few are those who grieve over the desolation of our order; fewer think about a remedy; very few supply assistance. Is the sacred order of Benedict, once the most excellent among all, thus not defended from the assault of enemies? Wake up, fathers, while watchfulness is of use, and do not repent too late that you have slept.

Look at the officials of other orders, how carefully, how zealously, how steadfastly they defend the rights, privileges, and monasteries of their religion, sparing neither expenses, nor labors, nor contributions, so that they may preserve their orders in vigor. Are you inferior to them? Are you poorer than the mendicants? If one wishes to consider the number of monasteries of the order, we are more numerous; if the substance of temporal goods, richer; if force and authority, undoubtedly more outstanding. What is lacking to us, except zeal and constancy, that they possess? Why then do we hesitate? Why are we ensnared in sluggish idleness? Why do we not keep watch for the defense of the order? Do you not know, fathers, that the laws assist those who are vigilant? It is not good patience by which the honor of God is neglected, the worship due to him is diminished, and the integrity of the holy order is violated.

What shall I say? You already grieve over monasteries that have been transferred, and yet you do not undertake to preserve those that are to be transferred. You put private things before common ones; for that reason your zeal bears little fruit. Each one of us, as I see, thinks himself safe if, when his neighbor’s house is burning, his own wall does not immediately grow hot. But O folly, O stupidity deservedly to be blamed. Whoever, entangled in so many dangers, is not stirred concerning his own safety, after a little while will be compelled, when he has fallen, to beat himself.

Therefore, fathers, if we desire to keep our houses unhurt by fire, let us meet the fire with water while it is still far away. For if the flame is allowed to pass as far as the neighboring places, thought is taken for a remedy much too late. Hence the poet says: Resist at the beginnings; medicine is prepared too late, when evils have grown strong through long delays. Dangers that are ignored are strengthened by time, and what in the beginning readily admits a cure gradually becomes an incurable wound. At the same time take care that an error, neglected in [unclear], does not in the course of time grow beyond measure, when no one is found who will steadfastly set himself against it on behalf of the order.

But if you say that opposition has likewise always been made to the authors of dismemberment, and that they nonetheless prevailed, I answer with that Virgilian saying: because the herdsmen came late. After the confirmation of letters, a Latin sentence is not easily recalled. For if Pilate was unwilling to change what he had once written, how will the supreme pontiff, the vicar of Christ, readily revoke a decree once made? A sentence is more easily prevented than revoked. Moreover, he who neglects his right yields to his adversary. All must keep watch in a case that touches all, because what is snatched from one is judged to have been taken from all. Whenever a monastery is seized from our order, our common inheritance is in part dissipated. If anyone should attempt to occupy your house or field, you at once accuse him before a judge, at once request an inhibition, and until you defeat your adversary you do not desist from the lawsuit. Why then do we all not do in the public causes of the order what each one does in private matters? Will that be impossible for many which one man does? Unless perhaps where there is a multitude, there is also confusion, so that what is entrusted to different persons is preserved more negligently. For we gladly embrace what each person commands to be nearest to himself. But while, with the body drawn together on every side, like a hedgehog, we turn over our own concerns within ourselves, we cast aside care for the order.

And so now, reverend fathers, with such goodwill as is fitting, I admonish you; with such attention as I can, I ask you: [unclear] for your order, which is nearly falling

run; and oppose these dismemberments as quickly as possible. Do not put money before such necessities; do not love coins more than the order. Shameful is the keeping of riches by which the commonwealth is not helped in necessity. What will an insatiable desire for gold profit you, if the desolation of your order, so holy, so venerable, so glorious, should prevail? If our predecessors had not kept watch for the order with greater care than we, the name of our religion would long ago have failed in many monasteries. Let us therefore imitate the constancy of those whose inheritance we have received. If we love God, if we love the honor of the order, if we desire to preserve it, let us think in time about a remedy. Let us contribute a little to the preservation of the order, so that we may deserve to receive much; let us spend a part, so that we may be able to preserve the whole; let us offer cheap things, so that we may be able to acquire precious things; let us give earthly things, so that we may be able to possess heavenly things. Let us expend money, and let us expend prayer also, since by the former man is appeased, by the latter God. Whatever we have belongs to the right of our holy father Benedict; when we expend something for him for the preservation of the order, we do not give him what is ours, but return to him what is his. Indeed, we are bound to him not only for the souls committed to us, but are also obliged to render account for the substance of the monastery. Never, moreover, is a safer account rendered concerning the [revenue?] than if money is spent opportunely in the causes of the Lord. But if money is spared in the Lord's necessity, suspicion is generated of the servant's faithlessness. At the beginning of this chapter we set down the title concerning the manner of resisting the dismemberments of the wicked; lest we seem to have passed it over untouched, let us explain it briefly. And although that discussion does not pertain to me, nevertheless, since I am a foster-child and lover of your chapter as well as of the same order, I think the admonition of a disciple will not be burdensome to you. It is for you, fathers, to distinguish the true from the false; let it suffice for me to have explained what I think about it. The manner of opposing the presumptions of monks is easily learned if it is turned from example into practice. Look at the other orders, and from their diligence it will be recognized what you must do. [Each?] establishes procurators of its own in the city of Rome, who manfully resist the beginnings of evils and permit nothing to gain strength against their order. And you, fathers, unless you do the like, will feel grave losses hereafter.

If therefore it can be done, if it is pleasing, let some man be chosen from the order, zealous, devout, learned, and experienced, who fights no less by favor than by zeal; who does not prefer his own advantages to public ones; who does not flee labors; who attempts nothing by his own rashness to be done contrary to the commission given him; who, established as procurator of the order, may always keep careful watch for it in the city. I believe that if such a man were had, he would forestall many dangers of the order. For it is the greatest foresight if a procurator in the city can denounce before the pope as false and fictitious the things which perverse monks lie as true for the sake of their own dismemberment. And this is not a work of great difficulty. For all the causes which they allege are full of fear and lying. But the vicar of Christ, who grants the transfers of monks more from importunity than from favor, when he has perceived that their allegations have been repelled by the diligence of our procurator, will rejoice that he has found an occasion for denying what he grants unwillingly. For he too fears the judgment of his Lord. Therefore, if we kept watch, we would have him as defender and advocate of our order. Our negligence alone is accused; our stinginess alone is condemned.

Against those who uselessly consume the goods of monasteries and scorn to assist the order even in a little. Chapter VI.

But now it is pleasing to turn the force of words against those who in such great necessities do not deign to assist the holy order even in a little. These are worldly abbots, useless, given over to pleasures, who, to use the words of the Mantuan, neglecting the worship of those above and spurning the command of the Thunderer, indulge Bacchus and serve Venus. They bear sacred things with gold, store coined money in gold; with gold they pour libations of wine, with gold the panelled ceilings gleam. They cover whores with gems; they set feasts for dogs; from the spoils of the needy they are adorned, rich by plunder, elated by success, and they laugh at the powers above and at Acheron. They have no care for the salvation of the soul; no love of God, no reverence for holy things, no exercise of virtues. These are the abbots rebellious against your chapter, who neglect the statutes, scorn the sanctions,

Now they despise [it]. From the lowly they have been made great, but they impiously despise the order that honors them. Saint Benedict raised you up, O ungrateful abbot; he made you rich. He received you as a monk. He appointed you shepherd of his brothers. Why then do you not acknowledge the munificence of your lawgiver? Why do you not repay his benefits in return? What do you have that you did not receive from his rule? Who endowed the monastery committed to you? Was it not the devotion of princes and the alms of faithful peoples? Why then are you ungrateful for such great benefits? Behold, you think of nothing less than regular observance. You reject discipline. You spurn God; you despise his precepts, and you presume upon security. Behold, contrary to the rule, you play with the birds of the air; behold, contrary to the law of clerics, you hunt with unclean dogs; behold, contrary to honesty, you take delight in the pleasures of the flesh; behold what is most shameful: despising the oath of chastity, you consume the substance of Saint Benedict with prostitutes and pimps. You do not fear to spend thirty or forty gold coins in the bath, and to offer Saint Benedict even one [unclear]. I lie if I have not known abbots who consumed more than fifty florins at the baths, of whom some are the first to resist the subsidies of the chapter. Others too, from among those who wish to be called observant, impatient of seclusion and quiet, unable to remain long in the monastery, consider every occasion suitable by which they can move from place to place at great expense. What shall I say of elaborate and superfluous building works, which are liable to no less censure than expense? The walls are adorned with paintings; the pinnacles gleam with gold; the windows are marked with memorials. The poor cry out at the door; the sacred order, hard pressed, asks for help, and no one deigns to give assistance. O abbot, servant of self-will, cultivator of vanity, enemy of piety, you who shamefully pour out the substance of the monastery, who pour wine in gold, who deny support to your order: how will the account of your stewardship be rendered to Saint Benedict? If the rich glutton was buried in hell because he did not, for God's sake, give help to Lazarus from his own goods, where will the abbot be buried who denied to his own lord what belonged to another? If he will burn forever who did not give alms from his own goods, what does the abbot deserve who has committed robbery? What do you have, O abbot, that you did not receive? For everything that you possess belongs to the right of Saint Benedict. Moreover, it is a moral rule for all that he who lives by the support of justice should dare to deny no one what is just. The definition of justice is to render to each person what is owed to him by right. But we who are placed in the monastery have nothing of our own; rather, in good faith we possess what belongs to another. What belongs to another is judged liable to restitution. For the gifts that princes and faithful peoples conferred upon monasteries for the support of monks are remembered as having been handed over to Saint Benedict. If, therefore, you have squandered his substance, if you have despised rendering to him what is his, you will be subject to a twofold damnation, since from unfaithfulness you will be judged sacrilegious, and from trust denied you will be judged criminal. Render, therefore, to each what is his, and do not usurp for yourself what is not yours. Give to your lawgiver his share, who bestowed the whole upon you. Why do you deny a little to him from whom you received much? Surely you will not be able to allege the poverty of your monastery, you who so shamefully consume so many things. I am ashamed to say what many abbots are not ashamed to do: they, not so much submerged in the pleasures of the flesh as maddened by them, preserve nothing of monastic honesty and omit nothing of worldly shamefulness. They think that all things are permitted to them, who [do not ask what is lawful, but] seek what pleases them. Behold, that one, abhorring monastic quiet, seeks solace in the world by wandering excursions. This one, impatient of regular seclusion, proceeds pompously in public. Another, disparaging the discipline of honesty, sits all day drunk as a companion with frivolous persons. This one, despising the meekness of the saints, involves himself in the cases of litigants. Another sits at the gaming table; another, [unclear], dances to the drum. What do ambitious abbots not presume? What pleasure do they pass by untried? As he dines, the knees of servants are bent. As he passes through the church, a whole [cloth?] is spread. As he goes forth in public, a great abundance of servants follows. You will find, I do not lie, an abbot even among those who boast in the name of reform, whose ambition is so great that he does not wish to be called inferior to a bishop; who at table with such great

... he resides in such [state?] that an abundance of vessels, a variety of food and drink, and a multitude of servants could suffice for any prince. Finally, if you should meet this man as he proceeds through the city, and see him surrounded by so great a multitude of servants, you would think that not an abbot but an archbishop was passing by. If they did not feign themselves poor, but were poor, they would by no means run to waste in such great solemnity of vanity. For I am certain that this crowd follows plunder, not the man. Who would expect to find plunder among the poor?

O abbot, runaway shepherd, ungrateful and unfaithful steward of the goods of your lord, who so uselessly expend the substance of the monastery; who live voluptuously and shamefully: who will help you at the final examination? Whom will you appoint as manager for the account that must be rendered? Behold, you consume the goods of Saint Benedict in pleasure; from them you assist your relatives; you lavish gifts on shameful men; you distribute presents to your flatterers; day and night you serve gluttony and drunkenness. You eat the richest things of the earth and drink the best wines; poor monks live in want; humble brothers eat the bread of sorrow; the sheep committed to you are fed on worthless things. O vain shepherd, who neglects the Lord's flock, who scorns the necessities of your brothers, remember to whom you are to render account; recall how dreadful it is to fall into the hands of the living God, who does not regard the person of man, who repays each one his reward according to his works.

But hear my counsel and do penance, and redeem your sins with alms; rather, absolve them by repayment of what is owed, so that before the inward judge you may deserve to find mercy. Lay aside haughtiness; cast off [unclear]; leave vanity behind. Be abbot of your brothers according to the Rule; be a shepherd in solicitude, a father in charity. Feed them with word; feed them with example; feed them with sustenance. If you omit one of these, you will be a useless shepherd; for without spiritual things temporal things avail nothing for eternal salvation; without the help of temporal things, spiritual things do not long subsist in this life. Therefore, if you wish to be a good shepherd, you must not deny that the care of both kinds of feeding, namely spiritual and bodily, has been laid upon you.

I had said that your sins must be loosed by repayment of a debt. Of what debt? That, namely, by which you are held bound to Saint Benedict. What is that? All that you have. For from him you have that you are a monk; from him that you are an abbot; from him that you are wealthy. Now, therefore, he from whom you have all these things knocks at your door; because of the necessity of his order he asks for help; he desires to receive the least portion from the greatest things that he has entrusted to you. Why do you deny him his own goods? Why, when they are demanded, do you not immediately restore what has been entrusted to you?

Divine Scripture commands and says: If you see the naked man, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh. Behold, your order is naked. Behold, your torn [origin?] cries out; it asks alms; it seeks back its own; it seeks help. If there are any bowels of compassion within you, if any inner sweetness, if any love of your order, if any love of God, do not despise your own flesh; do not scorn so great and public a necessity. Honor him who first honored you. Give alms to him who raised you up. Bestow a little on him who made you rich in many things. However much you give him, nothing at all is diminished for you, if only you bring a good will. You will give a little and receive much; you will bestow earthly things generously and hope for heavenly things.

Nor should it escape you that, as is commonly said, whatever is withdrawn from honor is reserved for disgrace. For the jurist says in his maxim: The treasury takes what Christ does not receive. He is not free from the guilt of crime who sets avarice before the piety owed to the order. If they despise the words of God, what wonder if they scorn ours? Although I may say many things, speak many things, urge excellent things, I shall never bend rebels by words to contribute to the order. Indeed, unless your authority, O presiding lords, intervenes, the speech of one who admonishes labors in vain. Therefore it belongs to your office to bend the rebellious; to you it is committed to humble the disobedient; ours is humbly to obey your sanctions. Therefore, if you desire to defend our order from the attacks of the wicked, take care first of all to recall the abbots to obedience, because unless unanimity is restored to the order, the wickedness of adversaries will easily prevail. For the Lord says in the Gospel: Every kingdom divided against itself will be desolated, and house will fall upon house. Division alone confounds the order. The treasury takes what Christ does not receive.

How disobedient and rebellious abbots are to be compelled to assist the order. Chapter 7.

If judges lack authority to restrain rebels, legislation will be made in vain. For we always strive after what is forbidden, and unless compelled we resist commands. For where there is no fear of power, the condition of law is quickly despised. Therefore the preservation of law is the fear of power. But where the laxity of power dissembles, the vigor of law totters. For a constitution, however holy or necessary, is quickly carried into oblivion if there is no authority by which contempt may be punished. Take away power, and the commonwealth will be nothing other than a confusion full of sedition. For rustic savagery is not led by reason, nor calmed by gentleness. Among our own too, may God amend it, there are many abbots and monks, coarser than rustics, more savage than beasts, who are not bent by gentleness to the observance of the commandments of God and of the Rule, and are never persuaded by exhortations, however holy. If the authority of superiors does not oppose these men, they will never be led by any obedience of the chapter.

For this reason the supreme pontiffs, founders of this most sacred provincial chapter, established for us many suitable remedies by which we can compel the abbots subject to the chapter to assist the order. We have authority; we hesitate about power. And what is authority worth without power? If you wish, most honored fathers, that I should say more openly what I have wished to depict concerning the power of authority, you will pardon me if I have noted your pusillanimity, not to say negligence. Behold, we know that one hundred twenty-seven abbeys have been placed under our provincial chapter, but we do not receive from all of them the subsidies of the contribution owed. Why is this? We have received authority to exact it, but we do not exercise power. We receive what is freely offered; we fear to compel the disobedient. For I am certain that many abbots of our province contribute nothing to the assistance of the order; indeed, if they are asked, they contradict as if by prescription. What is it that we are doing? Why do we dissemble so long? To one running of his own accord we apply spurs; to one lying down, indeed kicking back, we do not even apply lashes. From this is born contempt of our statutes; the authority of the chapter is despised; the inheritance of the order is everywhere laid waste.

These things are to be brought against you, O fathers, who neglect to subdue rebels at the beginning. Consider what this dissimulation is at last going to bring forth, and if you love your order, think as soon as possible about a remedy. Weak and near dissolution is the body that is deprived of the support of its members. Behold, from one hundred twenty-seven abbots, how few you see in the present chapter, all of whom ought by statute to have been present. Where are the rest, with all the procurators of the absent? Few have contributed to the necessity of the order; fewer keep the statutes of the order; very few have assembled at the chapter. Where are the letters of excuse of those who did not send procurators? Where are the double expenses of the rebels? Who of the absent and rebellious has ever in many years been compelled to pay the penalty of double, and [unclear]? What use are our statutes to us; what do laws do; what help are the privileges of the supreme pontiffs, if in time of necessity they are not put into practice? Behold, Pope Benedict XII provided for us suitably in all things, when he promulgated the restraints of censure to be imposed against the contumacious and rebellious. Why then do we delay? Why do we not put into practice against the disobedient the remedies granted to us? Truly, fathers, this dissimulation of ours that we practice is not praiseworthy. For the rebellion of a few, if dissembled, will be an occasion for many to resist. But if a few are compelled to obedience by discipline, the boldness of the multitude will be restrained by fear. Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and every religious order disagreeing with itself is gradually dissipated. There is no fair hope for an order where the confusion of unity is in tumult. For the first road to desolation in every commonwealth is the disobedience of subjects. Therefore, venerable fathers, if you desire to continue the provincial chapter; if you wish to oppose the dismemberments of monks; if finally you choose to defend your order from the hands of enemies, take care first of all to call the contumacious back to obedience, lest what you acquire outside by industry you lose within through the division of subjects. This indeed must first be attempted by the sweetest exhortations; but if with hardened neck they have despised these, they must be [met] with harsher rebukes

[unclear]. But if neither gentle measures nor harsh ones have taken care of them, then ecclesiastical censure is promulgated against them. For fools are not corrected by exhortations, but become proud. Yet in these matters measure must be observed, and necessary discretion, without which no rebellion is ever mitigated. For it is better to have weak sheep than none. But who is so fit that he may preserve discretion everywhere? It is difficult to apply measure to all deeds. But he who wishes to cure infirm souls must be both severe and pious, and, as it were, tempered from a certain mean between both, so that severity may not be excessive, nor piety slack. For the one breaks, the other dissolves. But the fairest manner of restraining rebels and the contumacious is that which the long experience of elders commends.

On Celebrating the Provincial Chapter. Chapter VIII.

When we have come together into one place, most excellent fathers, let us diligently investigate what the celebration of the provincial chapter requires. For the greatest force of our stability is placed in it, if it is celebrated rightly. For it is the sole stronghold of our order; without it our whole religion would be thrown into confusion, as is apparent in those who for many years have celebrated no chapters. For the chapter is the preservation of the order, the increase of regular discipline, the uniting of unity. For in it integrity is given to morals, purity is increased in minds, the quality of regular life [unclear]. But what does it require, that it may be celebrated rightly?

Hear what its sincere celebration demands. It requires zeal; it requires knowledge; it requires piety. Without these three the celebration of the chapter is worth nothing. For if zeal is lacking, who will rebuke the delinquent? If knowledge is lacking, what fruit will excessive [unclear] bear? Again, if piety is lacking, zeal does not sharpen, knowledge directs; piety produces fruit. Without zeal knowledge remains cold; without piety, fruitless. Likewise zeal without knowledge comes forth excessive and indiscreet, without piety hateful. But piety is of value for all things, although without zeal and knowledge it does not suffice for the governance of souls. For it pleases all; it benefits [unclear], apart from the humble. Therefore the whole matter of celebrating the chapter consists in the disposition of those presiding, which requires men who are zealous, learned, and gentle. For if they are remiss, if unskilled, if cruel and impious, how then will they reform others to piety? If he who sits to punish crimes admits them, whom, like himself, will he correct? Therefore this fault must be referred to you, fathers, if you have chosen deformed and vicious abbots for the presidency. Therefore take care with the greatest solicitude that you appoint such men to preside over the chapter as an irreproachable life commends, the zeal of holy religion sharpens, and instruction in saving knowledge tempers. For one who presides over others ought to be a man sound in morals, mature in conduct, instructed in knowledge of the Scriptures, adorned with gentleness. Such a man, O fathers, is deservedly to be preferred by us, whose life may provide an example, whose doctrine an increase of virtue. If the presidents of the chapter are such, those subject to it will easily be brought back to obedience. For those will be fit to preside who by word can instruct the teachable, by example the rude, and by authority the contumacious. In these ways indeed the chapter will be celebrated rightly, and the souls of subjects will also be edified. The other things that render presidents fit I am not permitted to describe on this occasion, since I believe none of them is ignorant what sort they ought to be. Therefore, O fathers, I turn to you again, you who have come together in this place for celebrating the chapter. I address you, I exhort you, that you direct your intention to the restoration of the order, and carefully consider why the chapter was instituted. Do you wish to know why chapters were instituted? Seek out the decrees of the supreme pontiffs, and the cause of their institution will be known. But lest either sloth or occupation impede the understanding of this matter, I shall briefly explain the occasion for the erection of the chapter instituted. For the Roman pontiffs and the presidents of general councils, seeing our order without a special remedy in obser-

Quāto em̄ crescit extꝑe: tanto minuitur inferuore: De- cedentibus nanqꝫ his qui ordinis zelum in opere demonstra- runt: abbates noui post eos surrexerunt: qui reformationis sanctum feruorem negligentes. in pristinas deformitates re-

that [observance?] could not long subsist: through a provincial chapter they decreed that aid should be given to it, in which, through the diligence of those presiding, all would be instructed to live according to the Rule, and no one could deviate from the reform once begun. For in a chapter of abbots vices are to be corrected; exhortations to virtues are to be made, so that the bad may find what they should fear, and the good may hear what may make them better. Therefore various things are read for edification, so that increases may always be present to good minds. There the abbot is instructed concerning his governance; there he is warned concerning the danger of pastoral care. There what he should do is commanded; what he should avoid is forbidden for the love of God. In short, when we come together thus for chapter, many useful things result, which, if we seek the salvation of souls, are very necessary. For, to pass over the rest, mutual acquaintance in charity is conceived there; experience shows how much this conduces to love of regular observance. There, from acquaintance, fraternal charity is both preserved and increased; otherwise it would quickly grow lukewarm if it did not have the nourishment of mutual recognition. Here easy access lies open to uniformity, where, by honorable conduct, from the mutual conference of the fathers a fire is prepared; from the fellowship of holiness an example is furnished. These are the camps of God, O fathers, and the strongholds of our order, by which all the devices of our adversaries are reduced to nothing. But there is not one sincerity in all; nor does equality of conduct appear among you. Whence could so great a disparity of manners have arisen in one order, where capitular unity is seen? Who has divided between you and the Rule of Saint Benedict, O fathers, long-haired with thick-grown hair? Why do you not look to uniformity, you who celebrate an assembly of unity? If you love the holy order which you profess, why do you not love uniformity in it? What is the use to you of the shadow of a hairy head? Whom do you think the height of a curled crown adorns, O ringlet-wearers? Believe me, fathers: a face covered with hair is reckoned a disgrace, not an honor, in a monk. O how beautiful this assembly would be, if it came together, as it ought, in one discipline of regular observance. What shall I say? I praise the assembly, but I rebuke the deformity in its members. For because of the confusion of the order, the presence of unity grows cheap. The outer habit judges that the inner clothing reproves the life of many. Truly, fathers, this disparity of manners and habits offends the provincial chapter not slightly; and it is known to have been instituted for this reason, that equality of life might be preserved above all things. For outward discord is an indication of inward discord. Therefore, so that we may be of one mind in observance of regular discipline, let us strive first of all to be conformed in habit and tonsure.

How necessary a diligent reform of the monasteries in our province would be. Chapter 9.

How necessary a diligent reform of the monasteries in our province may be, you yourselves know, O fathers, who are not ignorant of the condition of the monks of this time. I have known it as known to you, with how great labors, expenses, and sweats the fathers once reformed our order; concerning them we find memorials, both few and weak, in our age. But among all the reforms of our order in our province, three most recently shone forth before the rest: namely the Castellan, taking its name from Castellum; the Melk, from Melk; the Bursfeld, from Bursfeld. All these, as they were fervent in the beginning, so, gradually cooling again, they approach their end. For the first two, as if worn out with age, have been reduced to a small number. The last, however, which is also the later, because it is still younger, also seems to be more steadfast. Yet even it nevertheless now seems to grow cool again in certain of its members, and to decline back again toward the laxity of the former life. So once the Cluniac reform, known throughout the whole world, when it carried itself far and wide, gradually failed, as though its strength had been lost through expansion. For it is said in the proverb: everything that grows old is near destruction. For a reform, however celebrated or holy it may have been, unless it is often renewed through the diligence of prelates, gradually vanishes. For the more it grows with time, the more it is diminished in fervor. For when those who demonstrated zeal for the order in deed had died, new abbots arose after them who, neglecting the holy fervor of reform, [unclear] into the former deformities

they have fallen. And, to touch upon matters nearer at hand: where is that reform which Nicholas of Cusa, cardinal and legate, began with incredible zeal? Where are those terrible oaths of all the abbots of our province, by which they bound themselves to regular observance into the hands of the same cardinal, before the altar of Saint Stephen at Würzburg? Where is the promised regular observance? Behold, fathers, you have one hundred twenty-seven abbeys under your chapter; of these, from the three observances already mentioned, scarcely seventy have remained under reform. Yet there are, I do not doubt, some who think themselves excellently reformed; but their manner of life denies it. Would that the abbots would heed the threat, often repeated, of our holy lawgiver, in which he says that the government of souls is liable to a most exact accounting. Would that they compelled the sheep entrusted to them to the pastures of heavenly life, lest they themselves perish eternally with their sheep. Look at the manner of life of abbots as well as monks, reeking all around without the law of monastic propriety; of this, once known to me, it is shameful for me to speak, and dreadful for you, most reverend fathers, to hear. For the three vows of religion, which because of their excellence are called substantial, they care for no more than if they had never promised to observe them. They confound everything; they defile everything; they presume everything.

If we look to divine worship, they perform it so confusedly, so disorderly, so dissolutely, that neither do the words sound out their sense, nor the melody its proper tone. For they are devoid of all learning and of the good arts, so that they understand absolutely nothing of the things they sing. Hence it happens that without affection, without devotion, without the savor of inward sweetness, they do not so much discharge the canonical hours as confound them. In their hands the book of divine Scripture is never seen. The practice of edifying speech is never taken up. No account is ever taken of the formation of morals. The whole day is consumed in obscene rumors. All time is enslaved to games and feasting. No mention is ever made of reform. The madness of those at odds with one another rages, and among the cowls, peace having been broken, the monastery, with the law despised, [unclear] to insane lawsuits. Spears and sword are ready there, so that you would think what you see not a monastery but a stronghold of men at war.

Witnesses to their own possession, contrary to the statutes, contrary to the laws, contrary to the Rule, they each inhabit separate houses, in which they practice not the pursuits of monks but those of clerics. They neither fear God nor love him. They think nothing of the future life, since they put the concerns of the soul after the pleasures of the flesh. They do not read the Rule of monks; they do not heed the statutes; they despise the decrees of the fathers. They spurn the vow of poverty; they know nothing of chastity; they hold obedience in contempt. And would that, since they refuse to be chaste, they would at least deign to be continent. The filth of vices fumes all around; and what everyone knows, we alone, who are commanded to correct it, do not know. Why should I use many words? They commit so many, so great, so various illicit acts against the Rule of Saint Benedict that I would think it easier to establish a monk anew than to be able to amend the life of such men. For nothing of monastic propriety remains inviolate among them; instead everything lies neglected, everything despised, everything contemned and torn. Angers, quarrels, dissensions, envies, detractions, curses, oaths, insults, and things like these are not judged among them to be sins, because what is public has begun to be lawful. A place lies open to vices and crimes; virtue alone does not deserve admission. They laugh if anyone begins to give a discourse on penitence before them; and, as Mantuan says, they despise those above and Acheron alike. There is no fear of punishment, no dread of the judge. You would see among them, as if in the spring of all vices, pride, greed, lust, gluttony, sloth, anger, hatred, and every pleasure of the flesh abound; if they can grasp it, they rejoice; if they cannot, nevertheless they eagerly desire it. The oaths have collapsed in their filth, and, as though reason had been lost, they are unwilling to be called back to penitence.

O good God, to what great calamity has an order once exalted been brought, one which could deservedly have been preferred to all orders. O holy father Benedict, who once were so solicitous for your religion, why do you abandon us at the end? Why do you not look upon your inheritance? Why do you not come to the aid of your order, now already falling? Have you cast aside care for it?

Or has your soul come to abhor your sons? Help us. Come to our aid. Bring assistance, for never has your religious order been surrounded by such grave evils. Behold, it is destroyed from without by lovers of the world; behold, it is torn apart within by perverse monks, so that no one can easily discern which is the greater crime: for monasteries to be transferred into the hands of secular clerics, or to remain longer in the hands of such wicked monks.

Alas, holy father, what shall I say? You, when once instituting abbots, commanded them to be solicitous toward weak monks; now pastors have no care for the sheep, no diligence for the salvation of souls. All seek the things that are their own, and not those of Jesus Christ. Behold, father, your sons, having zeal, desire to come to the rescue, but they accomplish nothing, hindered by the rashness of the wicked.

Who, amid these things, will truly come to the aid? The bishop? But he cares for his own affairs; he seeks his own interests; he despises ours. The prince? But he sells favor, rejects discipline, seeks temporal things. There is no one who grieves over the ruin of your order, no one who comes to its aid, no one who renders assistance. All who can restore it neglect it; others who seem to have zeal for discipline try to help, but cannot.

O abbots, abbots, you who are the occasion of all evils in your monasteries, who, given over to vanities, do not at once correct delinquent monks: how harsh a sentence of damnation you will receive. To you, believe me, to you will be imputed the damnation of your monks, you who were set as their rulers and neglected to form their morals. Woe to you. It would be better if you had never been abbots. You, given over to avarice and lust, neglect the work of the Lord; you despise the care of souls; you think nothing of the path of observance.

You who ought to correct the vices of monks commit vices yourselves, and, lest your own be reproved, you pretend not to see those of others. You see, most honored fathers, what the state of your order is: what abbots, what monks; how those who might correct the wicked are lacking, and only those who quietly [unclear] among them come forward. Why, then, do you delay? Why do you not think about the reform of such men? Why do you not restrain the monks’ wicked pursuits? Their ill repute confounds us; their examples scandalize us, since the more numerous they are, the more [unclear]. Now then, father, come to the aid: they are your sons, your instituted ones.

[unclear] by those who do not know as preferable to action. Rise up, fathers, for the days are both short and evil. Reform, according to your powers, the order that has been deformed; raise up what has been cast down; restore what has collapsed. For unless you quickly apply a remedy, you will soon suffer grave harm.

For dissolute monks, enemies of regular discipline, always aspire to worse things, and, lest they be saved in the order, they strive to abandon it. For beginning reform you have the aids of law; you have the Rule; you have the statutes. This alone is required of you: that you put them into practice. Therefore, if you love your order, indeed because you love it, do not neglect it; do not delay, because the greatest necessity presses, since the impiety of perverse monks presumes everywhere. Behold, the rich of the world violently seize the goods of monasteries; behold, devotees of avarice invade the possessions of the order; behold, secular clerics receive the abbeys of Saint Benedict in commendam. None of these things would happen if abbots and monks had persevered in regular observance. Let us therefore impute to ourselves what we suffer, since we did not resist the rashness of wicked men from the beginning. To us, I say, this blame is justly ascribed, since, intent on our own advantages, we do not care for the losses of the order, as though they were another’s.

Rise up, I pray, fathers; rise up, even if late at last, after so many losses, after the perdition of so many souls, and let us do what lies within us, henceforth imploring the mercy of God, that he may supply what is lacking in us, direct our zeal, and bring holy endeavors to completion. And if we cannot bring the whole order back to unity of good conduct, let us strive at least to reform, [as far as possible?], those monks who are in our province. But if complete conformity cannot be had in all things, let them at least be reformed in three essentials, without which the life of monks is to be judged nothing other than the shameful brothel of an unfaithful soul.

Reform, moreover, must begin with the abbots, and thereafter be continued among the monks. For unless the shepherd has been brought back to sincerity, the health of the sheep will not endure long. For it is commonly said: when the head is sick, the other members suffer. Therefore every adornment of the body must begin from the head. There are certain unreformed abbots who, for the reform of

nachos suos velint compellere: sed ipsi obseruācie regulari. nec in minimo volunt subiacere: odio habētes in se bonum qđ in alijs diligunt: et quod subditos ꝓhibent. ꝑ se facere nō erubescunt. Talibꝰ o patres nolite confidere: ipsi sunt em̄ qui nos confundūt: visitationes spernūt. decreta capituloꝝ con temnūt. Faciat nos experientia cautos: quos zelos aliquan do sine scientia fecit penitentes. Quod visitatores ad reformatio- nem ordinis nostri debeant esse solliciti. Capl̓m .x. Is aūt reformationis maxima: pene industrium posita est. Idcirco dicitur in consti¬ tutionibus patrum: vt ad visitationis officium viri depurent idonei: qui vbo et exemplo ad ho¬ nestatem conversationis visitandos efficaciter possint instruuere. Oportet em̄ visitatorem doctum esse lege divina: opor¬ tet sanctum et irreprehēsibilem esse vita: vt verbo dociles: ex emplo instruat pertinaces. Nam unum sine altero in recto¬ re animarum nō sufficiet. Si em̄ ideota fuerit: quomodo ali¬ os informabit? Si cōuersatio bone actionis exemplum visi¬ tandis nō prebuerit: quomodo ad reformationem eos coar¬ tabit? Audiet sane obiectum prouerbij quo dicitur Medice. cura teip̄m. Nec immerito. Em̄uero qua p̄sumptione duce¬ ris o visitator poliloge: vt reformare alios temptes. q̇ad huc in deformitate ꝓpria iaces? Sordibꝰ vicioꝝ pollutꝰ es: et ali¬ os mūdare poteris? Crede mihi nō dabit spūssanciꝰ virtuteꝫ sermonibꝰ tuis: qui gratiā eius ꝑ contrariam vitā offendis. Caret efficacia sermo in corde auditoris: quem vituperat cō¬ versatio predicantis. Quid dicam? Mentior nisi contuma¬ ces contumax sepe increpat: turpis turpem infamat: et eua¬ sisse se conscīum credit: quasi cōscientia satis non sit. Sūt in quam inter eos qui vicia arguin̄t viciosi: in publico accusa¬ tiõs: quod si quis debeat esse visitator, debet habere hoc in animo: ut si quis debeat esse pastor, debet habere in animo hoc: ut si quis debeat esse magister, debet habere in animo p̃sumptione duce¬ris o visitator polilogē: vt reformare alios temptes. Et sic videtur que si quis debeat esse reformatorem ordinis nostri, debet habere in animo istas duas sententias: 1. Visitator est peritus in industria visitationis. 2. Visitator est instrumentus ad reformationem. Et sic videtur quod si quis debeat esse minister visitationis ordinis nostril, debet habere in animo idem duo motus: 1. Minister visitationis est peritus in industriā visitationis. 2. Minister visitationis est instrumentus ad reformationē. Et sic videtur quando quis debeat esse ministrem visitationis ordinis nostri, debat habere in animo idē duo motū: 1. Ministre visitationis est peritus ī industriā visitationi. 2. Ministre visitationis est instrumentus ī reformationē. Et sic viderit quando quis debeat esse officium visitationis ordinis nostri: debat habere in animō idē duo motum: 1. their monks to conform; but they themselves do not wish to be subject to regular observance even in the least. They hate in themselves the good which they love in others, and they are not ashamed to do themselves what they forbid their subjects to do. Do not trust such men, fathers: for they are the ones who confound us; they spurn visitations; they despise the decrees of chapters. Let experience make us cautious, whom zeal without knowledge has sometimes made repentant.

That visitors ought to be solicitous for the reform of our order. Chapter 10.

But the chief force of reform is placed almost entirely in diligence. Therefore it is said in the constitutions of the fathers that suitable men should be deputed to the office of visitation, who by word and example can effectively instruct those to be visited in honorable conduct. For a visitor must be learned in divine law; he must be holy and irreproachable in life, so that by word he may teach the teachable, and by example instruct the obstinate. For one without the other will not suffice in a ruler of souls. For if he is ignorant, how will he instruct others? If his conduct does not provide those to be visited with an example of good action, how will he compel them to reform? He will indeed hear the objection of the proverb, which says: Physician, heal yourself. And not undeservedly. For by what presumption are you led, O wordy visitor, that you attempt to reform others, while until now you lie in your own deformity? You are polluted with the filth of vices, and will you be able to cleanse others? Believe me: the Holy Spirit will not give power to your words, when by a contrary life you offend his grace. Speech lacks efficacy in the heart of the hearer when the conduct of the preacher condemns it. What shall I say? I lie if it is not often the disobedient man who rebukes the disobedient, the foul man who defames the foul man, and he believes that he has escaped the witness, as though conscience were not enough. There are, I say, among those who denounce vices, vicious men; in public, accusers: [unclear]

[unclear] in secret [unclear]; against themselves they are at once censors and offenders. They condemn outwardly what they do inwardly. They willingly commit what, once they have committed it, they make a crime. It is boldness wholly characteristic of revilers, and shamelessness befitting the shameless. Often the avaricious man rebukes the greedy, the lustful man the immodest, the proud man the haughty, the criminal the base. What, fathers, what do you think? Can deceivers of this kind be found even among the visitors themselves? I dare not say it; yet I have experience of it. Many say many things; few show in deeds what they speak. They cannot reform themselves and their own, and yet they strive to force others to observance. They say great things and do the smallest. Foolish presumption, which, neglecting its own affairs, is carried away to those of others. He who is not sufficient for himself, for whom will he be sufficient? He who cannot bring himself and his own to amendment of life, when will he be able to amend others? I have said these things against those who are such men, who condemn in others what they scorn to amend in themselves. But as for zealous, good, and suitable visitors, of whom I have known several, I would not wish anything to have been said as an injury. But you, most excellent fathers, who have to choose visitors, take care to appoint better men to that office, if you desire to bring monks to regular observance. For the whole of regular discipline lies with the visitors: when continued it grows; when neglected it fails. Indeed, if the visitors diligently fulfill their office, they will preserve reformed monasteries in regular observance, and will easily bring unreformed ones back to a better state. But if they are negligent, even things well begun by others they would quickly destroy. For nothing so confounds unity, nothing so disturbs peace, nothing so injures charity, as the ignorance of visitors. It grows heated not by reason but by an undiscerning will. Experience has very often taught us what great disturbances, dissensions, angers, quarrels, slanders, and hatreds unskilled visitors have stirred up in congregations of monks: men for whom everything consists in command, and nothing in knowledge and charity. But I have said enough about this, lest I seem to accuse those whom, because of the dignity of their office, we are commanded to treat with honor.

How Dangerous the Government of Souls Is. Chapter XI.

If we considered how dangerous a thing the government of souls is, how heavy the burden of pastoral care, how subject it is to strict examination, it would be a wonder if ever in this life our heart presumed upon security. For Scripture says that very hard judgment will be made upon those who preside. For, as blessed Benedict attests in the Rule, the abbot will have to render an account to God for the souls of all the monks entrusted to him. Therefore he says: Let the abbot who has been ordained always consider what a burden he has undertaken, and to whom he will render an account of his stewardship. Certainly it is both a heavy and dangerous burden to render an account for the souls of many, since each person can scarcely answer for himself. O what will abbots devoted to earthly things answer to the supreme shepherd, who destroy the souls of their brothers by evil example, and feed them neither by word nor by deed? What shall I say about certain abbots of our order, who neither read the Rule of Saint Benedict which they profess, nor, if they read it, understand it? I would be lying if I said that I did not know abbots established under our chapter who are wrapped in such darkness of ignorance that they do not understand even the smallest sentence from the Rule. They neither know nor love the divine Scriptures; submerged in the vanities of the world, they vanish away, serving the desires of the flesh and not of the spirit. According to the precept of our lawgiver, the abbot ought to be learned in the divine law, so that he may know and have a source from which to bring forth new things and old; chaste, sober, merciful, and so forth. What will these men say, what will they teach, what exhortation will they give, who understand nothing of the holy Scriptures, nothing of regular discipline? O good God, to what misery our order has come, which once was full of most learned and most holy men. Where now is love of regular observance? Where is study of the Scriptures? Where do we find the traces of honorable conduct? Our abbots, with few exceptions, either given over to avarice or bound fast by the vanities of the world, think of nothing less than knowledge of the Scriptures, although

many may consider them learned. But from their works the learning of their intellect is recognized. Now the greedy man is believed learned; now he is called religious who joins field to field, who keeps watch over earthly gains, who loosens his appetite for gathering riches. But believe me, fathers, since I am going to speak the truth: temporal riches do not make discipline stable in the order. O what a terrible sentence abbots will undergo: those who neglect the Rule, who do not go before their monks in word and by the example of holiness, who despise spiritual exercises, who devote themselves to earthly gains, who scorn the discipline of monastic honor. Would that they were wise and understood, and foresaw the last things; and either governed carefully the burden of so great a rule, or, if they could not, humbly laid it down. Happy is he who stands solicitous upon his watch, who always does the will of the Lord, who lives without pretense according to the purity of the Rule.

But for the present these things which we have said concerning the state and reformation of our order, as I believe, are sufficient; let the reading of them also obtain its end at the same boundary as the chapter. Moreover, all and each of the things which I have written in this treatise or in others, or shall write, I submit to the examination of the sacrosanct Roman Church, whose faith, doctrine, and definition, so long as I live, I wish always and everywhere to observe, teach, and defend. But if anything, which God forbid, has been said by me otherwise than she holds, teaches, and believes, I now by these presents simply revoke it, and wish it to be regarded as not said. By this my protestation I wish and hold the supreme pontiff, the vicar of Christ, to be in all things the judge and moderator of my faith and doctrine.

The present treatise was read in the provincial chapter of the order of Saint Benedict of the province of Mainz, celebrated at Hirsau at table, in the year of the Lord 1493, on Jubilate Sunday and on the following days until the end. With all the abbots gathered there wishing and consenting, it was decreed that it should be printed and in future provincial chapters always be read publicly at table, as is clear in the statutes.
